```{r}
renv::load()
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
pubs_data <- read.csv('data/PubMed_Timeline_Results_by_Year.csv', skip = 1)
```

## Meta-analysis Overview

**Short answer**: Formal meta-analysis provides statistical methodoology to pool data 
from multiple individual experiments or trials to synthesize a combined estimate of a 
population parameter. This turnes out to be quite useful in biomedicine, because if one 
is working on an interesting question others probably are working on it too, and often 
there are multiple studies looking at similar things in relatively similar ways.  

Many have also done probably tried to a similar thing informally. For example, a common 
practice for powering Phase II starts with looking at historical trials that are similar, 
creating a spreadsheet of the effect size and variability and ballparking some consensus 
estimate.  That means that the overarching concept is probably intuitive; the statistical 
tools and the overarching process just provide substantially more rigor when understanidng 
the accuracy and precision of that consensus estimate really matters.

```{r}
p_pubs <- pubs_data |>
    filter(Year != 2027)|>
    ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = Count))

p_pubs + 
    geom_col(fill = 'blue') +
    labs(
        title = "Systematic Literature Review and Meta-analysis Publications Indexed in Pubmed",
        x = 'Year of Publication',
        y = 'Number of Publications',
        caption = "Based on data retrieved on November 21, 2026."
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```


Below are some specific scenarios for which meta-analysis is often applied with varying
methodologies.

**Scenario 1**: Multiple studies measuring the same thing in similar ways

When one runs an experiment or analyzes data from a clinical trial, individiual measurements 
are combined to provide parameter estimates. Because the number of experimental subjects or 
trial participants is small relative to the entire population, such estimates will have varying 
degrees of precision. In this case, the parameter estimates represent a single 'sample' from a 
hypothetical population of similar studies that measure similar things.  Each of such studies 
might estimate the parameter differently due to random noise but one would probably expect the 
results of those hypothetical similar studies to be roughly in the same ball park. If one 
actually had data from that population of studies, one might and probably would want to combine 
or pool the results in some way to better separate an estimate of the true parameter from within 
and between study variability.
